title: Hare Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bija, Ganesha's seed in Om Gam Ganapataye, said at the door of beginnings. Your line was clear the road. Today, a mantra that's meant to be sung.

A group walks down a city street, in London or New York or Sydney, in saffron and white, with a drum and small hand cymbals, singing. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna. People stare, or smile, or cross the street. It can look like something new. It isn't. That same song filled the streets of a town in Bengal in the fifteen-hundreds, sung by a man who, his followers say, danced until he fell to the ground. And the words themselves are older still.
screen: `A DRUM AND CYMBALS DOWNTOWN.` → `IT LOOKS NEW. IT ISN'T.` → `A TOWN IN BENGAL, THE 1500S.`

segments.voice: Here are the words. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Sixteen words, only three names. Krishna, the one you followed from the prison at midnight to the chariot. Rama, the prince who came home to a city of lamps. And Hare, which many devotees understand as calling on Hara, Radha, the love and energy of God, and which others hear as a form of Hari, Vishnu, the one who takes away. That's the maha-mantra, the great mantra. It appears, with the Rama half first, in a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, which says that in this age, the simplest way across is the name. Then, in the early fifteen-hundreds, in Navadvip in Bengal, came Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. His followers remember him as Krishna himself, come as a devotee, taking the names out of quiet rooms and into the street. Singing together, with drums and cymbals, is called sankirtan, and Chaitanya made it the heart of the practice. Why out loud? His tradition says the name isn't just a word about God; it carries God. Sung, it reaches everyone in earshot, even the ones crossing the street. In 1965, a monk in his line, an elderly man named A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, arrived in New York with almost nothing. Before long he was singing it in a city park. That's where the group you saw comes from. The name, out loud.
screen: `SIXTEEN WORDS, THREE NAMES.` · `THE SIMPLEST WAY ACROSS.` · `CHAITANYA TAKES IT TO THE STREET.` · `1965: A MONK IN NEW YORK.` · then, large: `THE NAME, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: This one isn't whispered: if you're somewhere you can, sing it softly, to any simple tune or on one note. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Once through is one round; keep going, and tap your knee for a drum if you like. If you don't pray, let it simply be singing, and notice what singing does that speaking doesn't; if you can't make noise, mouth the words.
Hare Krishna. The maha-mantra: sixteen words, three names, meant to be sung out loud.
Your line: the name, out loud. Some words are meant to be heard. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including members of ISKCON, chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra daily on beads, often sixteen rounds of 108, and sing it together in kirtan with drums and cymbals, at home, in temples and in the street.

notes: In the Kali-Santarana Upanishad the mantra begins 'Hare Rama Hare Rama…'; the Gaudiya order (starting 'Hare Krishna') is the one taught here. A Keeper may want this noted in the script.
'Hare' as vocative of Hara (Radha) is the Gaudiya reading; as a form of Hari (Vishnu) is another. Both given without ranking. Confirm.
Chaitanya (1486–1534) in Navadvip; his followers regard him as Krishna appearing as a devotee (with Radha's mood). Confirm wording.

Bhaktivedanta Swami arrived in New York in September 1965 and first chanted in Tompkins Square Park in 1966; the script says he 'started singing it in a park' after arriving, compressing the timeline. Confirm.
Krishna glossed in the original note as 'the dark one, the all-attractive' (the second is the Gaudiya reading). Confirm.
